encryption.sealed_copies_notice: Verified encrypted copies protect backup artifacts, not the running SQLite database. Run `php cron.php --seal` and then `php cron.php --recovery-drill` from the server after setup. The drill decrypts and validates current copies without touching live data; schedule seals separately. Recovery requires the private key outside the web root and an explicit CLI restore.
encryption.bootstrap_recovery_notice: Bootstrap configuration recovery is deliberately CLI-only: `scripts/restore-config.php` authenticates and parses the sealed PHP without executing it, atomically replaces `lib/config.php`, and leaves the prior configuration as a sealed rollback artifact. Test the recovered settings before deleting that artifact.
encryption.superseded_copies_notice: Superseded copies remain encrypted with an earlier local key after rotation. Keep that key until you have completed a replacement-key recovery drill; they are not deleted automatically.

setup.help.openid_enabled: Lets explicitly registered trusted applications sign users in through this Zogograph installation. It does not make this server a public identity service.
setup.help.openid_issuer: The HTTPS URL trusted clients use to discover this provider, for example https://monitor.example.com. Do not include a trailing slash.
setup.help.openid_signing_private_key: Required before enabling the provider. Use a dedicated RSA private key; never reuse the TLS certificate key. Setup can generate a dedicated key that is kept only in the protected setup session until this section is saved.
setup.help.scan_root: Everything is measured under here, and nothing outside it can ever be deleted.
setup.help.timezone: Used for the timestamps on the dashboard and in alert emails.
setup.help.encryption_mode: Off keeps all current storage unencrypted. Sealed copies make separately encrypted, verified snapshots; they do not alter the live database or its journal. Host-managed volume protection is configured and operated outside Zogograph.
setup.help.package_runtime_trusted_keys: Optional. Add only a publisher key you independently trust. Each key id maps to a publisher name and Base64 Ed25519 public_key. A signed package cannot install unless its publisher and key match this list.
setup.help.package_runtime_secret_key_fi: An absolute private key file outside this web directory. Leave blank to reuse the local encryption key when configured. Without either key, package secret references cannot be saved. A separate file gives package credentials separate custody.
setup.help.encryption_key_custody: The built-in sealed-copy mode currently uses one private local key file. Fleet, manual-unlock, and marketplace key providers will be selectable only when their secure protocols are installed and tested.
setup.help.encryption_key_file: Create it first with scripts/encryption-key.php. It must be an absolute, non-symlink file outside this web directory and readable only by the Zogograph service account.
setup.help.encryption_artifact_directory: Leave blank for data/sealed. Use an absolute private path to keep encrypted copies elsewhere.
setup.help.encryption_stores: The recommended start protects bootstrap configuration, setup, and account data. Add host or assistant stores when you want their process evidence or conversations protected too; those optional stores wait until they exist.
setup.help.encryption_backup_schedule: Zogograph records this preference; configure the matching cron or host-scheduler job. Manual creates copies only when cron.php --seal is run.
setup.help.encryption_retention_days: Zero means keep every copy. During an explicit sealing run, Zogograph prunes only old verified local artifacts whose ciphertext hash still matches, and never the newest verified copy for a store.
setup.help.encryption_retention_days_by_: Optional JSON object, for example {"setup":365,"account":30}. Zero keeps every copy for that store. Stores not listed use the normal retention target.
setup.help.encryption_recovery_drill_max: Zogograph warns when a selected store has not completed a non-destructive recovery drill within this period. Ninety days is the recommended starting point; zero disables periodic reminders after the first required drill.
setup.help.encryption_retention_recovery: Optional JSON object such as {"daily":7,"weekly":4,"monthly":12}. It preserves the newest verified copy from each distinct UTC day, week, or month in addition to normal retention. Zero or omitted tiers keep the simple retention target.
setup.help.password: Reveals real paths and enables deleting. Leave blank to disable sign-in, which leaves the dashboard readable with every path masked.
setup.help.alerts_enabled: The point of the thing: it tells you before the disk fills, not after.
setup.help.alerts_from: Blank uses whatever the server sends as by default.
setup.help.disk_free_bytes: Write it how you say it: 5G, 500M, or a plain number of bytes.
setup.help.projected_full_hours: Fitted over the last day of readings. This is the alert that arrives while there is still time to do something.
setup.help.path_jump_bytes: The alert that names the culprit rather than the symptom.
setup.help.cpu_percent: Sustained, not a spike: it has to hold across the whole window below. Zero turns it off. On CloudLinux this is a share of what the account may use, not of the machine.
setup.help.cpu_minutes: A burst cannot hold across a long window, which is the whole point of measuring duration rather than height.
setup.help.cooldown_seconds: Written how you say it: 6h, 90m, 2d. A plain number is seconds. An alert that arrives every minute becomes a filter rule within a day.
setup.help.anomalies_enabled: Compares each service, category and file against its own history. It catches the things no threshold can - a job that normally takes two minutes still running after an hour - and stays quiet about the nightly backup that always grows. Says nothing until it has history to say it from.
setup.help.anomalies_min_readings: Below this it says nothing at all. Too low and its first day is all false alarms, which is how these get turned off.
setup.help.anomalies_service_percent: Against its own median over the last day, not against a fixed size. A service that grows and stays grown is leaking; one that grows and comes back was busy.
setup.help.deletable_categories: Only ever by a signed-in session, and only inside the watched directory.
setup.help.host_enabled: Adds a second collector, run by root from WHM, that sees what this account cannot: other users' processes and memory, kernel slab caches, and root-owned logs under /etc. On CloudLinux this is the only way to find out what is using the machine.
setup.help.core_features_assistant: Disabling this removes the assistant from the dashboard and blocks its API routes. Existing assistant settings and private data are retained for a later re-enable.
setup.help.core_features_overview: Disabling this removes the Overview dashboard and its shared measurements. The shell keeps only the feature and access state needed to open another enabled page; collection continues unchanged.
setup.help.core_features_peers: Disabling this removes trusted servers from the dashboard and refuses its API, telemetry, and connection routes. Existing peer settings and private data are retained for a later re-enable.
setup.help.core_features_marketplace: Disabling this removes Marketplace from the dashboard and blocks its API routes. Installed marketplace metadata and revision history are retained for a later re-enable.
setup.help.core_features_terminal: Disabling this removes the Terminal and its sessions from the dashboard, blocks its API routes, and prevents assistant tools from reading terminal history. Existing private terminal evidence is retained for a later re-enable.
setup.help.core_features_notes: Disabling this removes notes, database copies, chart annotations, and broadcasts from the dashboard and blocks their API routes. Existing notes and captured evidence are retained for a later re-enable.
setup.help.core_features_problems: Disabling this removes Recent problems, its dashboard badges, and its API routes. Zogograph continues recording server errors so diagnostics and support remain safe.
setup.help.core_features_storage: Disabling this removes account storage, its file views, data controls, and retention controls from the dashboard; blocks their read, management, and assistant APIs; and preserves scans, configured retention, and safe server-side rollups.
setup.help.core_features_audit: Disabling this removes the Audit page and blocks its API routes and assistant history tool. Zogograph continues recording accountability entries server-side.
setup.help.core_features_metadata: Disabling this removes Custom names and What things are from the dashboard and blocks their API routes. Existing labels and descriptions are retained for a later re-enable.
setup.help.core_features_notifications: Disabling this removes Email alerts from the dashboard and blocks its configuration and test API routes. Existing alert delivery settings and server-side alert evaluation continue unchanged.
setup.help.core_features_backups: Disabling this removes the Backup inspection pages and blocks their API route. It does not alter backups or their provider-managed schedules.
setup.help.core_features_encryption: Disabling this removes Protection and blocks its on-demand status and recovery APIs. Configured encrypted-copy schedules and server-side verification continue unchanged.
setup.help.core_features_alerts: Disabling this removes Alerts, its shared dashboard badge and banner, and its API routes. Server-side alert evaluation and configured delivery continue unchanged.
setup.help.core_features_uptime: Disabling this removes Uptime and blocks its API route. It does not alter host or account collector schedules.
setup.help.core_features_packages: Disabling this removes Package runtime and package-contributed pages from the dashboard, blocks package-management APIs, and stops loading package language catalogs. Installed package records and their private settings remain intact for a later re-enable.
setup.help.core_features_charts: Disabling this removes Over time, blocks chart catalog and series APIs, and prevents assistant chart tools from reading or rendering chart history. Collectors and the current overview remain available.
setup.help.core_features_health: Disabling this removes the System health and self-diagnostic dashboard, blocks its presentation and diagnosis APIs, and hides overview findings. Setup checks and server-side collector safety checks continue to run.
setup.help.core_features_network: Disabling this removes network views and blocks their API, outbound lookup, capture, URL/domain, reverse-DNS, and calendar actions. Existing outbound safety, allow-list, and rate-limit controls remain enforced whenever it is enabled.
setup.help.core_features_host: Disabling this removes host, CPU, process, filesystem, capability, and change views; blocks their APIs, assistant tools, and on-demand host-task requests. Root-owned collection and its configured schedule continue unchanged.
setup.help.host_owner: Root creates the host database, so without this only root can read it and the panel stays empty. Almost always the cPanel username.
setup.help.host_watch: Apache writes each domain's logs under /etc owned by root, where a rotated log can reach several hundred megabytes invisibly. Shell globs.
setup.help.host_keep_days: A host reading is much bigger than an account one - it carries every user, the biggest processes and the slab table.

Ciphertext replica storage remains a separate future capability. Never enter a custody or relay management token, billing credential, plaintext database, or recovery key into this client.
cpu.limit_faults: {{faults, number}} CPU fault(s) recorded at the last reading across {{accounts, number}} account(s). A fault is an account asking for more processor than its LVE allows and being held back — this is being throttled now, not being near a limit. A throttled account's own percentage sits calmly at its ceiling, which is why the fault count is the figure to watch and not the percentage.
cpu.limit_throttled: This account is at {{account, number}}% of its own allowance while the machine is {{host, number}}% busy. That is not a contradiction: the two percentages have different denominators. It is the ordinary shape of hitting a limit, and it is felt as a slow site even though the server has plenty of processor left.
cpu.limit_comparison: This account is using {{account, number}}% of what it is allowed; the machine as a whole is {{host, number}}% busy. Neither number is a share of the other, and dividing them produces nothing meaningful.
cpu.limit_missing_side: Both halves of this comparison need a reading — one from this account and one from the host collector running as root.

cpu.last_ten_seconds: share of the last ten seconds

cpu.process_summary: {{processes, number}} processes using the processor, adding up to {{percent, number}}% of one core{{machine}}{{busy}}.
cpu.process_summary_busy: , against {{percent, number}}% measured across all cores
cpu.spread_not_measured: No per-core percentages yet. Each one is a difference between two readings, so the first collection after this feature was added has nothing to compare against.
cpu.spread_one_core: One core, so there is no distribution to look at — the whole-machine figure is the core's figure.
cpu.spread_shape: Busiest core {{busiest, number}}%, quietest {{quietest, number}}%, {{average, number}}% on average across {{cores, number}} cores.
cpu.spread_all_pinned: {{shape}} Every core is pinned: the machine has no processor headroom at all. Unlike a single busy core this does respond to more cores — but it is worth checking first that the work is work you wanted done.
cpu.spread_single_threaded: {{shape}} That is the shape of a single-threaded bottleneck: one piece of work that cannot be split, holding things up while the machine looks mostly free. The whole-machine percentage will never look alarming however stuck it gets, and more cores would not move it.

cpu.spread_uneven: {{shape}} Uneven, but not one core carrying everything — normal on a machine running a mixture of jobs, and worth a second look if the gap keeps widening.

storage.masked_names: Names are hidden until you sign in. The sizes and the growth are real.
tree.help: Area is size. A directory full of small files is invisible in a list of the biggest paths and obvious here, because forty thousand session files add up to a large rectangle even though not one of them is large. Click a rectangle for its details, double-click a directory to go into it, hover for a quick summary. Filtering to one type shrinks every directory to just the files of that kind inside it, which is how you find where the audio is.

backup.share_unknown: Share of the disk unknown — no filesystem reading recorded.
backup.walk_incomplete: The disk walk ran out of time, so this total is a lower bound.
backup.directories_not_opened: {{count}} directories under the backup roots were never opened.
backup.unattributed_help: Some of this could not be tied to an account. Nothing under the backup root carried a name matching a directory in /home, and JetBackup's own records were not readable — so it is reported as unattributed rather than assigned to the only account on the machine, which would be a guess.
backup.inferred_accounts_help: Accounts inferred from directory names under the backup root — JetBackup's own metadata was not readable, so these are a reasonable guess rather than its records.
backup.unmeasured_entries_help: {{count}} entries here could not be measured before the walk ran out of time. They are listed with no size rather than omitted. Raise host.walk_seconds and run it again for a complete figure.
backup.other_help: Directories that look like backups but are not managed by anything: a tar.gz somebody made before an upgrade, a dated copy of a site, a database dump. Nothing rotates these, so they stay for ever and are usually the oldest large thing on the disk. Probable is the operative word — each is a guess from the name and shape, and worth looking at before acting.
backup.safe_actions: Safe — returns space the backup system already considers disposable
backup.review_actions: Worth reviewing — a decision, not a chore
backup.dangerous_actions: Dangerous — listed so it can be named, not recommended
terminal.unavailable_reason: {{reason}} There is nothing this page can do about that, and nothing it should try — a host that has taken shell functions away has taken them away on purpose.
terminal.switched_off_help: The terminal is switched off. It is off by default because it runs whatever is typed into it — that is not a reason to avoid it, but it is a reason for the decision to be deliberate rather than inherited from a sample file.
ai.memory_written_in_conversation: Written by the assistant in conversation {{id}}.
ai.memory_empty: {{name}} has not written anything down yet. It does that on its own when it works something out that will still be true next month — and you can add one yourself with the button above.
ai.memory_capacity: {{count}} memories out of a possible {{maximum}}. Past that, the least useful are dropped — pinning one keeps it whatever happens.
ai.memory_subject_edit_help: The subject is the key, so it cannot be changed — forget this one and write a new one if it is wrong.
ai.memory_subject_help: A short phrase. Writing the same subject again replaces what is stored under it.
ai.memory_remember_help: Written for somebody with none of the conversation it came from — no “as we discussed”, and say what it was based on.
backup.no_suggestions: Nothing to suggest from this reading.
backup.storage_help: Backups are usually the largest thing on a server and the last place anybody looks, because they are not in /home. This asks four questions: how much space, whose, how old, and what is safe to do about it.
backup.actions_title: What can be done about it
backup.actions_help: Sorted by how safe each one is, not by how much it would free. Anything marked destructive removes the only copy of something — the whole point of a backup is that it is there on the day nobody expected to need it.
backup.jetbackup_help: What the backup system says about its own backups is the only place the account and date behind a directory called files0000000005 can be found. It needs the JetBackup command line tool and usually needs running as root.
network.ports_public_empty: Nothing is listening on an address reachable from outside.
network.public_risky_port_tip: This normally has no authentication by default. Reachable from off the machine, that is a serious exposure rather than a configuration choice.
network.peers_empty: No established connections were recorded. Either the machine is idle, or ss could not be run by the collector.
network.private_address: a private address — another machine on this network
network.captures_empty: No captures have been taken yet. Ask for one on What is on the wire.
network.own_label_tip: A name you gave this, under Settings → Your own names.
network.rdns_name_tip: What the internet says this address is called — a PTR record, which its owner controls and can set to anything.
network.rdns_waiting_tip: Waiting to be looked up. One is resolved per collector run.
network.rdns_none_tip: Looked up: this address has no PTR record, so it has no name to show. That is a real answer, not a failure.
network.rdns_ask_tip: Queue a reverse lookup for this address
network.rdns_queued_tip: Queued. One is resolved per collector run.
network.rdns_taken_tip: A collector has already taken this one
network.rdns_no_name_tip: The address resolved, and the answer is that it has no PTR record. That is a real answer and is remembered, so it is not asked again for a week.
network.rdns_stale_tip: Older than {{age}}. Ask again to refresh it.
network.rdns_ask_again_tip: Queue another lookup — names do change

uptime.track_last_late: last one {{duration}} ago — later than usual
chart.compaction_bucket: Each point covers {{duration}} and shows the worst value in that period, not an average.
chart.compaction_disk: The oldest readings here are also compacted on disk, up to {{readings, number}} readings to a row. Readings from around an alert are never compacted.
host.swap_verdict_pressure: Swap is climbing ({{swap}}) while available memory falls ({{available}}). Those two together are real pressure rather than leftover cold pages — the machine is paying for memory with disk. This is the one worth acting on.
host.swap_verdict_filling: Swap is growing ({{swap}}), but available memory is holding steady. That is the kernel moving cold pages out of the way, not the machine running short.
host.swap_verdict_cold: Old or cold pages left over from an earlier squeeze. Linux does not pull pages back out of swap just because RAM frees up, so this figure stays where it is until something touches them — a high-water mark, not a measure of now. No current shortage: watch for swap rising while available memory falls, which is a different thing entirely.
host.swap_verdict_waiting: Not enough readings yet to say whether this is left over or still growing — that needs about half an hour of history.
host.memory_pie_empty: No measured process memory in the latest reading
host.memory_pie_help: Share of measured process memory. Drawn from PSS because a pie claims its slices make a whole, and resident memory cannot — a page shared by ten processes would be counted ten times and every slice inflated.
host.memory_pie_total: Total {{amount}} across the {{processes, number}} biggest processes. The ten largest services get a slice; everything under 1%, and everything past the tenth, is folded into one.
host.services_no_history: No service history yet — this needs a few readings to build up.
host.services_chart_empty: Not enough service history to draw yet
host.services_counter_rate_help: Counters differentiated into a rate; a gap means the service restarted.
host.io_stacked_tip: A volume mapped onto another device. Its traffic is already counted there, so it is not added into any total.
host.io_collector_missing: The host collector is not installed.
host.io_needs_two_readings: Needs two host readings before a rate can be worked out.
host.io_no_counters: No device counters recorded for this range.
host.io_busiest_moment: Busiest moment: {{rate}} at {{at}} — the busiest device was {{saturation}}% saturated.
host.io_counter_restarts: {{readings, number}} readings could not be turned into a rate, because the counters restarted — that is a reboot.
host.mount_points_more_tip: The same filesystem is mounted in these places too. Bind mounts, so the space is counted once.
host.mount_points_help: One filesystem, mounted in several places. The disk holds these bytes once — which is why this table shows one row rather than one per mount point.
host.deleted_open_help: These files have been unlinked but a process still has them open, so the blocks stay allocated. df counts them; du, ls, find and the treemap cannot see them. Restarting the process listed frees the space.
host.deleted_none: None — no process is holding space in a deleted file.
host.deleted_root_only: This needs /proc/<pid>/fd, which only root can read. Run the host collector to fill it in.
host.directories_none: Nothing recorded. Ask for a walk from the Storage page.
host.gap_incomplete_help: The walk ran out of time, so “found” is a lower bound and the gap is an upper one. Raise host.walk_seconds and run it again before chasing the difference.
host.walk_pending: A walk was requested {{ago}} and is waiting for the next host collection. It runs on the collector's schedule — every five minutes with the suggested crontab line.
host.walk_requested: Requested. The host collector will walk the disk on its next run.
host.daemon_stopped_all_readings_tip: Stopped for every reading on record, so this was almost certainly disabled deliberately rather than having failed. It does not raise alerts.
host.daemon_not_watched_tip: Switched off here, so the collector is not recording it. Nothing is known about whether it is running.
host.daemon_waiting_tip: Switched on, but the collector has not run since. It reports on its own schedule.
host.daemon_not_installed_tip: Neither a systemd unit nor a running process by any of the names this service is known by. Almost certainly not installed on this machine.
host.daemon_cannot_tell_tip: systemd could not be asked and no matching process is running. Stopped and never-installed look identical from a process list.
host.daemon_stopped_tip: This was running earlier and is not now.
host.daemon_since_state: Since this state was first seen here.
host.daemon_at_least_this_long: At least this long — it has been this way for every reading on record.
host.daemon_stop_watching_tip: Stop recording this service. Its history is kept, but nothing more is added and it will not raise alerts.
host.daemon_watch_tip: Start recording this service again from the collector's next run.
host.daemon_stop_watching_notice: {{service}} will stop being recorded at the next host reading.
host.daemon_watch_notice: {{service}} will be recorded again at the next host reading.

host.memory_card_available_help: the kernel's estimate of what is left
host.memory_card_other_kernel_help: not represented by the categories above
host.cloudlinux_help: A process killed for hitting an LVE limit leaves no other trace. A rising fault count is the evidence.
host.services_time_help: One line per service, from the host collector's own longer-lived record. This is the panel that answers “and what was it in June?”
host.memory_by_user_help: The column CageFS hides. Inside a cage this account sees only its own processes, so who else is using the machine's memory is unanswerable from anywhere but here.
host.memory_by_user_pss_help: The column CageFS hides. {{pss}} counts a process's private memory {{full}} and divides each shared page among the processes using it — so one copy of libc shared by a hundred workers contributes a hundredth to each, while everything that process alone holds counts whole. That makes it the effective physical memory attributable to a process, and the one figure you can add up. {{resident}} counts every shared page once per process, so it always totals more than the machine has. The {{kernel_shared}} card above measures something else again — tmpfs and System V segments — and is not a subtotal of this column: a tmpfs page some process maps is counted in both, and one that nothing maps is counted only there.

diagnostics.title: What is wrong
diagnostics.help: There are forty pages here, each answering one question well — which helps when you already know the question. This reads all of them at once. Every line carries the measurement it came from and a link to the page that shows it in full, and nothing here is inferred from a correlation.
host.capabilities_title: What the host allows this account
host.capabilities_help: On a shared host the numbers above are the cage's answers. Inside CageFS this account is shown a /proc written for it: its CPU allowance looks like the machine's cores and its memory limit looks like the machine's RAM. Comparing both readings is the only way to tell a limit from the size of the server.
overview.went_at_once: {{amount}} went at once, not a trend
host.memory_breakdown_help: The share of measured process memory each service holds, drawn from {{pss}} rather than {{rss}} — a pie claims its slices make a whole, and resident memory cannot: a page shared by ten processes would be counted ten times.
host.memory_processes_help: Every process on the machine, not just this account's. This is the list that answers ‘what is actually holding the memory’ when the per-user totals only say whose it is.
host.kernel_slab_help: Memory the kernel holds for itself. It belongs to no process and no account, and it is the first place to look when the numbers do not add up — a quarter of a gigabyte of xfs_inode appears in nothing else on this site.
host.services_alive_help: The one question the rest of this page cannot answer. A daemon that has died uses no memory, no CPU and no disk, so it vanishes from every chart above rather than standing out in one. {{not_installed}} is shown apart from {{stopped}} on purpose — a service this machine never ran is not a fault, and colouring it red would make the panel permanently alarming and therefore ignored.
host.big_directories_help: From root's walk of the whole disk, so this reaches the places the account cannot: other accounts' homes, /var, /backup, and anything mounted somewhere unexpected.
host.disk_processes_help: Which processes the throughput is actually coming from. CPU can sit low while one job makes everything else feel slow by keeping a disk busy, and that job is invisible in every other panel on this site.
host.root_files_help: Apache writes each domain's logs under /etc owned by root. A rotated log there costs exactly as much disk as one in the home directory and is invisible to everything the account can run.
host.filesystems_title: Filesystems, and the space nothing accounts for
host.filesystems_help: For when {{df}} reports a number nothing else can explain. Every filesystem root can see, and the gap between what the filesystem says is used and what walking it actually found. The two usual explanations have pages of their own: {{deleted}} and {{directories}}.
host.deleted_held_help: A file that has been unlinked while a process still has it open keeps its blocks. {{df}} counts them; {{du}}, {{ls}}, {{find}} and the tree map cannot see them at all. This is the one kind of missing space no directory walk can ever find, and restarting the process listed is what frees it.
host.cagefs_help: CageFS gives each account its own {{usr}}, {{lib}} and {{proc}}, assembled from a shared skeleton at {{skeleton}}. That is why a program the server has can be missing from inside the account, and why this dashboard's view of the machine is narrower than the machine. From inside a cage the skeleton's own mounts are invisible — so an empty answer here is not evidence that CageFS is absent, and this says which of the two it is looking at.
host.processes_help: Running right now, with processes of the same name added together. ‘Running for’ is the oldest of the group — a long-lived pool whose newest member is seconds old is restarting as fast as it dies. Arguments that look like passwords are hidden.
processes.trend_title: Reported process load over this range
processes.trend_initial_help: The newest reported processes lead this list, with high peaks retained so a process that has settled down is still visible. Names group replacement workers together; PIDs are intentionally not a chart identity.
processes.stop_help: For when the name is not specific enough to aim with — twelve {{webalizer}} processes where one of them is chewing through one particular log. This is {{pkill}}, with the two differences that matter: the pattern is matched here rather than handed to a shell, and it shows you what it would hit before it hits anything.
host.last_busy_help: Recorded automatically whenever a reading crosses the CPU or memory threshold — so an overnight spike still has an answer in the morning. The collector and the {{ps}} it runs are left out: a record of a busy moment listing the thing that looks at processes is noise by construction.
host.last_busy_allowance_help: {{allowance}} Inside CageFS {{proc_stat}} is virtualised to the account's own CPU allowance, so one PHP request working hard can cross 70% while the server as a whole is idle. Raise {{threshold}} if these are too frequent to be interesting; {{whole_machine}} is where the server's own load lives.
network.intro: Every other page here measures something being used up — disk, memory, CPU — and none of them can say why. A machine pinned at 100% because it is answering four thousand DNS queries a second looks exactly like a machine pinned at 100% for any other reason, and the difference is only visible on the wire.
network.open_ports_help: What is listening, and what usually answers on each port. A port number is a convention rather than a fact — anything may bind 443 — so the service column is the expectation and the process column is the reality. Where they disagree, that disagreement is the interesting thing.
network.peers_help: Established connections grouped by the address at the other end. Grouped because the useful shape is ‘one address is holding nine hundred sockets’, which a flat list of nine hundred rows states without showing.
network.capture_help: The tool of last resort, and treated as one: it opens a live interface as root, runs for as long as you ask, and is the only thing this collector does that could itself be felt on a busy machine. It records counts and endpoints only — how many packets, between which addresses, on which ports, and for DNS the names asked for. No packet contents are stored, ever.
network.dns_help: Run when you open this page rather than read from a record — ‘was it working five minutes ago’ is never the question. A nameserver that is busy and answering is a completely different situation from one that is busy and timing out, and only asking it can tell them apart.
network.capture_history_help: Every capture that has been taken. One report answers ‘what is happening now’; two an hour apart answer ‘is this getting worse’, which is usually the real question. Rates are shown rather than totals, because two samples of different lengths cannot be compared any other way.
network.url_checks_help: Everything else here watches the machine from the inside, which cannot answer the question a visitor is asking. A server can be healthy by every internal measure and still return 500 because a config file is wrong, or return 200 with an empty page because a database is down — nothing in {{proc}} knows. These are checked from this machine, so they cannot tell you the site is unreachable from somewhere else.
network.fetch_help: One request, made now, reported in full — what the server actually sends, which is the question while you are setting a check up or arguing with a cache. Type an address with or without {{https}}. The body is shown as text and never inserted as markup; the preview runs in a sandboxed frame of its own, which can neither read this page nor act as you. The body is kept for an hour so the preview can load it, then discarded.
network.rdns_title: What the internet calls an address
network.rdns_help: A capture or an access log is a wall of numbers, and the same number means nothing on Monday and something on Friday once somebody has looked it up. This is not {{labels}} — that is what you decided an address means, and is small, hand-written and permanent. This is what the internet says it is: automatic, occasionally wrong, and stale within months.
host.units_help: The whole list, not just the watched ones. {{failed}} and {{masked}} are called out because they are the two states that are silently wrong: a failed unit uses no memory and no CPU, so it is absent from every other panel here rather than standing out in one, and a masked one cannot be started at all until somebody unmasks it.
log.stream_help: A machine misbehaving does not tell you which log to open. This is all of them merged, newest first, because the line that explains it is the most recent one somewhere.
calendar.upcoming_help: Three months back and twelve forward. Domain expiries and the projected full-disk date are worked out here; renewals, invoices and anything else only you know about are the ones you add. Behind us: the critical alerts that fired, so ‘what changed around then’ has an answer.
network.domains_help: A domain expiring is the one outage nothing else here can see coming. Disk, memory, CPU and the HTTP checks all stay green right up to the moment the name stops resolving, and then everything fails at once for a reason that is in no log. Checked weekly — a registration does not change between Tuesdays, and whois servers throttle anybody who asks more often.
network.whois_help: A one-off lookup for a name you are not watching — whether it is taken, who holds it, when it expires. Nothing is stored and no domain is added to the list; there is a button for that if the answer makes you want one.
network.dns_records_help: A name resolving is not the same as a zone being right. Mail stops arriving because an MX was dropped or an SPF edited; a subdomain starts pointing somewhere that is not yours; a TTL cut to sixty seconds during a migration is never put back. None of that shows anywhere else here. Names come from a zone transfer where your nameserver allows one, from cPanel's own record of this account's domains, and from what was found last time — not from guessing at names.
network.dns_change_help: A record that stops resolving is kept and marked gone rather than deleted — ‘the MX disappeared last Tuesday’ is the question somebody asks a week later, and a deleted row cannot answer it.
system.whoami_help: Two identities that get confused constantly: the browser at the other end, and the account this process runs as. The second is the one that answers permission questions — ‘this account cannot read that’ means nothing until you know which account it is.
cpu.title: CPU
cpu.help: How hard the processor is working, and how much of it this account may use. Inside CageFS the account's own percentage is of its allowance rather than of the machine, so a pinned account and an idle server are the ordinary shape of hitting a limit rather than a contradiction.
cpu.findings_help: Every line below is a measurement taken from this machine, with a link to the page it came from. Nothing here infers a cause it cannot see, and ‘nothing found’ is said in those words rather than as a clean bill of health.
cpu.busy_title: Busy, and what it was busy with
cpu.busy_help: The total busy line is split into the states that make it up. The monitor tree and the remaining workload are also shown: together they explain the total, while alerts continue to use total host CPU. Percentages are of every core added together, so 100% is the whole machine occupied rather than one core of it.
cpu.time_help: A processor is never simply ‘busy’. Every jiffy it spends is charged to one of eight states, and which one decides what to do next — work in userland is the machine earning its keep, time in the kernel is a syscall-heavy workload, iowait is a disk problem wearing a CPU costume, and steal is the hypervisor and not you at all. The single busy percentage everywhere else on this dashboard is all of these added up and is the reason the question usually gets asked twice.
cpu.cores_help: The distribution the average has already thrown away. Eight cores at 12% and one core at 100% beside seven idle ones are the same whole-machine reading and completely different problems: the second is a single-threaded bottleneck, it will never make the overall percentage look alarming however stuck it gets, and buying more cores makes it exactly as slow as it was.
cpu.cores_history_title: Hottest, coolest and average, over time
cpu.cores_history_help: Three lines rather than one per core: on a machine with thirty-two of them the individual lines are a legend rather than a chart. The gap between the top line and the bottom one is the whole finding — when it is wide the work is not spreading, and when the three sit together the machine is loaded evenly and the only question left is how much.
cpu.procs_help: Processor use per process, read as root, so this is every account on the machine and not only this one. Percentages here are of {{core}}, the way {{top}} reports them — a process with four busy threads shows 400%, which is a fact about it rather than an error. That is the opposite convention to every other percentage on these pages, and the columns say so.
cpu.procs_visibility_help: A process is only here if it was alive for two consecutive readings or has burned real time since it started. Work that arrives and leaves inside one minute — a fork-per-request server, a tight cron loop — can hold a core permanently without a single one of its processes ever appearing in this table. If the machine is busy and this list is not, {{fork_rate}} is where that shows up.
cpu.queue_help: Why a load average of 40 can sit on a machine that is 5% busy. Load is a queue length, not a processor reading: it counts everything runnable {{and}} everything stuck in uninterruptible sleep waiting on storage, so a hung disk drives it into the dozens while the cores idle. These are the figures that tell those two apart.
cpu.queue_chart_title: The queue, and the load average beside it
cpu.rates_title: Context switches, interrupts and new processes
cpu.rates_help: The counters that explain a machine which is busy while nothing on it looks busy. A high fork rate with an empty process table means the work is arriving and leaving between readings. Context switches climbing without more work arriving means time is going into scheduling rather than into the jobs being scheduled.
cpu.limits_help: The page for ‘the CPU is pinned and the server is idle’, which is not a contradiction and not a broken reading. On shared hosting this account is given a slice of the machine and told, through a percentage of its own allowance, how much of that slice it is using. Both numbers are correct and they measure different things; nothing useful comes of comparing them as a ratio, so this page puts them side by side instead.
cpu.lve_title: Where the ceiling was actually hit
cpu.lve_help: CloudLinux records a fault every time an account asks for more processor than its LVE allows and is held back. This is the difference between ‘we are near the limit’ and ‘we are being throttled right now’, and it is the only figure here that says so directly — a throttled account’s own CPU percentage sits at its ceiling and looks calm.
capabilities.title: Capabilities
capabilities.help: What this account can actually run, and what the machine has that it cannot reach. Those are the same question on ordinary hosting and different ones here — see below.
alerts.title: Alerts
uptime.title: Uptime and outages
uptime.gaps_help: A hole in the readings is not the same as the machine being off, and the charts distinguish them — {{restart_shading}} where the boot time moved, so it really did restart, and {{gap_shading}} where the boot time was unchanged either side and the collector simply was not running. Uptime counts only the first kind; a cron job that stops should not look like a server that keeps falling over.
uptime.restart_help: A {{restart_line}} marks each restart the host knows about from {{last}}. Those need not leave a hole at all — a reboot the collector resumes after within a minute has nothing to shade — and they include restarts from before boot times were being recorded, which the readings alone cannot show.
uptime.restart_explanation: Boot time moved, so the machine did restart. It came back at {{booted}}; it went down at some point after the last reading, so this is an upper bound rather than a measurement.
uptime.gap_collector_not_running: Boot time was unchanged either side, so the machine ran straight through this — it was up, and the collector was not running.
uptime.gap_before_tracking: These readings predate boot-time recording, so whether the machine restarted here cannot be told. Not an outage — just a stretch that cannot be classified. Gaps from now on will say which.
uptime.gap_unknown: No boot time either side to compare, so whether the machine stayed up through this cannot be told from these readings.
uptime.no_gaps_or_restarts: Every reading in this window is present and the machine never restarted. Nothing to explain.
uptime.boot_history_help: From {{last}} on the host, which only root can read. A boot with a shutdown recorded before it was asked to stop; a boot with none means the previous session ended without recording one.
audit.title: Everything this monitor has done
audit.help: Every deletion, every scan, every request to the host collector, every email it sent, every configuration change and every sign-in — whether each worked or not. A refusal is kept as carefully as a success: knowing what was {{not}} done is half of knowing what happened.
email.title: Email alerts
email.help: Mail goes out through PHP’s {{mail}}, which on a cPanel host means the server’s own mail queue. One message per alerting run rather than one per rule — a disk filling up trips several rules at once, and five separate emails about the same event is how people learn to ignore them. The message takes the volume of its loudest line, lists them loudest first, links each one to the page that answers it, and ends with the commands to diagnose the same thing from a shell — because the most likely moment for this dashboard to be unreachable is the moment the disk is full, which is exactly when its email arrives.
email.settings_sign_in: Sign in to change the email settings.
system.monitor_help: A disk monitor should be able to answer for its own disk use, and should never stop collecting without saying so. Neither is visible anywhere else on this site: a database quietly growing to a gigabyte looks exactly like one that is fine, and a cron job that stopped last Tuesday just makes every chart look quiet.
system.health_help: What this install can and cannot do. The first three are the usual reason a fresh deployment returns errors.
health.data_dir_writable_help: The database cannot be created or updated.
health.php_new_enough_help: This code will not run correctly.
health.sqlite_help: Nothing can be stored at all.
health.mail_available_help: Alert emails cannot be sent from here.
health.shell_available_help: Inodes and the crontab editor are unavailable.
health.proc_readable_help: CPU, memory and network stay empty.
health.no_inline_styles_help: index.html carries a style="" attribute, which the content security policy blocks — the rule silently does not apply. Move it into index.css.
health.diskstats_readable_help: Disk I/O throughput and utilisation stay empty.
ai.identity_help: {{assistant}} is a model you configure, given a fixed set of read-only tools for looking at this machine — the name is the job: somebody on watch who tells you what they can see. It is off until you set it up, and when it is on this tool sends parts of your logs, your disk figures and your process list to whichever service you point it at — which is worth deciding deliberately rather than discovering. A local model needs no key and nothing leaves the machine.
ai.identity_security_help: The model can never write a query. Every tool is a fixed statement with typed, enumerated parameters bound to it, and anything outside those bounds is refused before it reaches a database. The rest of the settings are on the pages under this one.
ai.model_help: Choose a platform and an available model. Prices are per million tokens, in cents, and optional — without them everything still works and the running total reports token counts rather than money, because a wrong price is worse than no price.
ai.providers_help: Choose the platform, its endpoint, and any credentials it needs. Ollama-compatible servers may use no key; remote ones must use HTTPS.
ai.review_page_requested: {{assistant}} asked for the current page structure.
ai.review_page_help: Review this before sending it. Delete or replace any element or text you do not want shared.
ai.chat_add_help: It is working. This goes in now and it reads it on its next turn.
ai.prices_help: Models and prices this install has been told about, per provider. Changing the selected model fills its price boxes from here rather than making you look them up again — and a model you have used before keeps whatever you set for it. Nothing here is fetched from anywhere: these are the numbers you were quoted, which is the only honest source for them.
ai.limits_help: What stops a conversation, and how much of one the model can hold at a time. Every limit here is checked before a request rather than after, so it stops the next call rather than being noticed once the money is gone.
ai.images_help: Entirely optional, and off until keyed. Generating a picture costs money; searching for an animation is a free read against somebody else’s quota. They are limited separately for that reason.
ai.try_help: Runs one tool with parameters you choose and shows exactly what comes back — the same thing the model would receive, in the same shape. Useful for two things: seeing whether a tool actually works on this install before switching it on, and reading what the model is being told when its answer looks wrong. Nothing here involves the model and nothing leaves the machine.
ai.billing_help: Every conversation, with the tokens it used and what that came to. Costs are shown only when prices are set — without them this reports token counts and no money, because a wrong price is worse than no price.
system.changed_help: Almost every {{working_yesterday}} turns out to be something changing underneath — a kernel that came with a package update, an OpenSSL bump that moved a default, a PHP point release that deprecated a function. None of it shows in any other chart here, and the machine does not keep a usable note of it either: the package log belongs to root, is not always present, and records what was {{installed}} rather than what is now answering. Every time on this page is when a change was {{noticed}}, not when it happened — this runs when capabilities are checked, so a weekly check turns a Tuesday upgrade into a Sunday event.
system.changed_groups_help: Each bar counts the programs whose availability or version moved, coloured by group. Click one to see exactly what. This was on {{capabilities}}, which is a page about what is available {{now}}; a history of changes belongs beside the rest of the history.
system.installed_help: What each thing is at this moment, and how long it has been that way. Where a program offers no readable version — and plenty do not — a fingerprint of the file stands in: a weaker fact than {{version}}, but the same kind of fact, and the only one available.
system.installed_history_help: This is the present tense of {{changed}}, and the two answer different questions: this one is what you are running, that one is when it started being that. Both are filled in by the same check — {{capabilities}} is where it runs.
notes.title: Notes
notes.keep_pictures_help: Saved with the note exactly as they are drawn now, so the picture still shows what you saw after retention has rolled the readings up underneath it.
notes.no_page_charts: There are no charts on this page.
notes.no_page_charts_help: The note itself is saved either way, and a mark on this page will show on any chart added here later.
notes.help: Every chart here answers {{what}}. None of them answer {{why}}, and the why is almost never in the data — it is that somebody upgraded PHP on the Tuesday, or that the backup window moved. Six months later the chart still shows the step and nobody remembers the reason. A note is pinned to a moment and drawn on the charts it belongs to.
system.snapshots_help: Forensic copies, written beside the databases and deliberately outside every retention rule — the point of one is to survive the roll-up that would otherwise discard the readings it is about. Which also means nothing expires them, so they are listed here for somebody to look at.
system.snapshot_empty: No copies have been made. One is written when a note asks for it — a consistent copy of both databases, for looking at after the readings it is about have been rolled up.
system.snapshot_delete_confirm:
Delete {{name}}?

It is {{size}} and nothing else has a copy.
database.host_unreadable: Present but not readable by this account, or not there at all.
database.indexes_note: Indexes are counted against the table they belong to. On a busy table an index can be close to half the total, and listing them separately makes every table look cheaper than it is.
system.peers_help: A trusted server is explicitly configured here and checked through HTTPS OpenID Connect discovery. Saving it does not share data or sign anyone in; those authorization-code steps are deliberately separate.
system.marketplace_help: Local package manifests only. Enabling never executes package code. A few fixed, core-owned capabilities may be authorized; requested capabilities remain visible for review.
system.encryption_help: This page reports Zogograph evidence, not assumptions. It never shows key paths or key material. Change protection choices in the setup wizard; recovery and sealing stay CLI-only so a browser session cannot handle a private key.
system.package_runtime_help: Signed packages are reviewed here before any future runtime can use them. Enabling records explicit capability grants and private-package settings; it does not execute package PHP in this Zogograph release.
system.problems_help: This dashboard’s own log. When a request fails it shows you a reference — find the same reference here for what actually happened. Identical faults are counted together rather than listed each time: the dashboard polls, every poll calls the API, and one broken function becomes forty lines in a minute.
reports.title: Summaries
reports.help: Written on a schedule by {{assistant}} from a fixed set of figures for the period — the same questions every time, so two summaries can be compared. What varies is what it makes of them. Each one is emailed when it is written; this is where they are kept.
terminal.title: Terminal
terminal.help: This runs what you type, as the user the web server runs as, and shows the output. Be clear-eyed about what that means: anybody who has the dashboard password has this, so it stays off until somebody switches it on here, and every command is written to the action log before it runs. Each command is its own process; the directory it runs in carries over between them and is shown above the box, so {{cd}} works and you can see where you are. What does not carry over is anything else a shell remembers — variables, functions, background jobs — because there is no shell sitting between requests to remember them.
terminal.interactive_help: It is a transcript, not a screen. Colour, bold, tabs and progress lines that rewrite themselves all render. Text editors such as {{vi}} and {{nano}} open a constrained browser editor instead. Programs that need an interactive terminal — {{top}}, {{ssh}}, or anything asking for a password — cannot be driven from here.
terminal.sessions_grouping_help: Commands that were run close together, grouped the way the work actually happened — an hour’s gap starts a new one, because somebody who ran three commands, went to lunch and came back was doing two different things.
terminal.sessions_topic_help: Give one a topic and it becomes something you can come back to. A list of timestamps is a list nobody reads; ‘the disk filling on Tuesday’ is a thing you look for six weeks later.
terminal.sessions_output_help: Opening a session shows what was run. What each command {{printed}} is behind its own switch, because those are two different questions with two different answers: what you typed is safe on any screen, and what came back may be a config file with a password in it.
terminal.sessions_empty: Nothing yet. A session starts the first time a command is run and stays open until an hour goes by without one.
ai.memory_help: A conversation ends and everything worked out in it goes with it. These are the things kept on purpose — which of the installed PHP versions the site actually runs, what the 03:10 spike turns out to be, how you have said you want to be told things. Everything here is editable and deletable by you, and every one records the conversation it came from, because a remembered claim whose origin cannot be found is a rumour.
ai.data_help: Kept apart from the account’s own database on purpose: everything here is a record of what was sent to somebody else’s service and what came back, and that is worth being able to read, export or delete without touching the readings. It is also the one database here that grows by conversation rather than by schedule — a long session with a few screenshots in it can outweigh a week of measurements — so what it is holding is worth being able to see.
storage.account_help: A monitor that fills the disk it is watching has failed in the most embarrassing way available to it. This is what this account’s database holds, what each part of it costs, and — the part that is usually missing — what the file will settle at if nobody touches the settings again. A table set to keep 400 days that has been collecting for thirty is at under a tenth of its eventual size, and nothing else here says so.
storage.host_help: Written by root’s collector, and read-only from here. This account can usually open it to read and should never be the thing that rewrites it — a rewrite started from here would leave a file the collector could no longer write. Where it cannot be opened at all, that is said rather than shown as zeros.
storage.retention_help: Zero means {{forever}}, and for several of these that is the recommendation rather than an oversight — the note beside each one says what it is protecting. Readings are kept in tiers: full detail for the first stretch, then five-minute buckets, then hourly, then daily, each holding the worst moment in its bucket rather than an average. Nothing within a couple of hours of an alert is ever rolled up or cleared, whatever these say.
storage.symlinks_help: The scanner steps over every symlink it meets, deliberately — following one double-counts at best and walks out of the watched directory at worst. The consequence is that a bad link is invisible to this tool while still being the thing that ruins everything else: a link pointing at one of its own ancestors is an infinitely deep directory to anything that {{does}} follow links, and backups, {{du}}, {{tar}} and web crawlers all do. That is how a disk fills up with one file copied ten thousand times.
storage.link_sweep_help: When a directory of dangling links is the problem, ticking four hundred boxes is not a workflow. Name a directory and everything {{broken}} under it goes, however deep — you do not need to know how many levels there are, and you should not have to add a {{star}} until the count comes out right. Working links under the same path are left alone and counted: the destructive half is bounded by a fact about each link, not by how carefully the path was typed. You are always shown exactly what would go before anything does.
screenshot.drag_selected: Drag it to move, drag a corner to resize, or press Delete to remove it.
screenshot.drag_redact: Drag a box over anything that should not be sent. You can move, resize or remove it afterwards — nothing is fixed until you send.
screenshot.drag_crop: Drag a box around the part worth sending. Everything outside it is left out, and you can undo it.
host_request.asked_with_cadence: Asked {{time}}. The collector runs about every {{cadence}}.
host_request.asked_unknown_cadence: Asked {{time}}. The collector's schedule is not known yet.
charts.help: The five measurements that describe the machine as a whole, over whatever range is selected. The gauges on the overview say where each one is {{now}}; these say how it got there, which is the half that tells you whether it is going to be a problem.
charts.room_help: Disk space and inodes. Either can run out on its own — a disk with free gigabytes and no inodes still refuses to create a file.
charts.cpu_help: Share of what this account may use, since the previous reading.
charts.io_help: Bytes actually reaching a disk, not bytes served from cache.
charts.load_help: Not a percentage: it is how many processes wanted to run at once. Compare it to the core count — at one per core the machine is busy, above that work is queueing.
charts.network_help: Bytes a second in and out, summed over the real interfaces. Loopback is not counted.
storage.whole_machine_help: A second walk, run by root, that reaches everything this account cannot — other accounts, {{var}}, {{backup}}, and space held by deleted files still open. It takes tens of seconds, so it is not part of the per-minute collection: pressing this leaves a request that the host collector picks up on its next run. The results are under {{filesystems}}, {{directories}} and {{deleted}}.
storage.type_title: What the space is made of
storage.type_help: Every file counted once, by extension, from the last completed scan. This is a different question from the categories below: those are the rules that raise alerts and let you empty things, and most files match none of them. These add up to the whole account, which is what makes the pie mean anything. {{other}} is files with no extension or an unfamiliar one, and on most accounts it is large.
storage.other_help: The extensions that matched no group, heaviest first. This is where a backup convention nobody documented turns up — {{bkup}}, {{old}}, a date-stamped copy of a database. {{none}} is files with no extension at all.
storage.type_growth_help: One line per type across every completed scan in this range. A type with no line had nothing of that kind at the time — the line starts where the first file did, rather than running along the axis from the beginning.
storage.categories_time_help: Totals from each completed scan. {{error_log}} files are counted on their own, wherever they turn up — one of them can be the whole problem.
storage.path_hygiene_help: An optional, advisory check that runs during the account disk walk. It does not send notifications. Rename only paths you recognize; the change is immediate and recorded in the audit log.
host.memory_overview_help: From {{cron}}, run by root. Inside CageFS this account gets its own {{proc}} holding only its own processes, so everything below is invisible to every other panel on this site. The detail sits on the pages beneath this one; what is here is the state of the machine's memory at a glance. Its disks are under {{storage}}, and whether its daemons are alive is under {{services}}.
host.io_title: How hard the disks are working
host.io_help: Throughput and saturation per device, read by root — so this is every account on the server together. A busy line here says the disk is working, never that this account is the reason; the account's own traffic is on {{dashboard}}, and {{processes}} has its own page.
host.io_disks_help: Throughput and how close each device is to saturated. LVM and RAID volumes are shown but not added into any total: a write to {{dm0}} is remapped onto the disk underneath and advances both counters, so summing them reports twice the traffic that happened.
host.layout_help: Every mount the kernel reports, grouped by filesystem. Two paths on the same device are the same disk however different they look, which is why a bind mount can make one directory appear to be two — and why summing mount points reports the same space twice. The skeleton's own mounts used to be the second half of this page and are now on {{cagefs}}, which is where somebody looking for them goes.
auth.sign_in_help: Reveals real paths and enables deleting.
log.repeat_help: A log filling a disk is almost never full of interesting distinct events; it is one event ten thousand times. These are the same lines with their variable parts — numbers, addresses, paths, quoted strings — taken out and counted, which is the only presentation of that fact anybody can act on.
calendar.saved_dates_help: Marked {{important}} means it appears on the dashboard and in the alert emails as it approaches, until you mark it dealt with. Marking it dealt with is reversible — it is a claim somebody makes, and sometimes makes wrongly.

assistant.interrupt_title: Stop what it is doing, keep the conversation
assistant.hide_title: Hide this — the conversation carries on
audit.download_csv_title: Download the full audit history as a CSV file
audit.clear_title: Remove earlier audit entries and retain a record of this reset
assistant.microphone_unavailable: Speech recognition is not available in this browser.
host_setup.line_to_paste_as_root: The line to paste, as root
host_setup.no_host_account: If you do not have a host account
host_setup.no_root_help: No root? The collector runs as an ordinary account too. It collects less, and here is exactly what less means.
host_setup.database_readable: Working. The collector's database is at {{database}} and this account can read it.
host_setup.database_unreadable: The database exists at {{database}} but this account cannot read it — which is the ownership step below.
host_setup.collector_never_run: The collector has never run. Nothing on this site that describes the whole machine will have anything in it until it does.
scan.set_up_title: This one needs choosing before it can be asked for
scan.ask_title: It happens on the collector's next pass, not now
scan.boost_while_browsing: speed up to every {{interval}} while somebody is looking
scan.request_withdrawn: Request withdrawn. The collector will not run it.
scan.request_already_completed: The collector had already answered that one.
setup.config_not_writable: lib/config.php is not writable, so these cannot change.
collector.settings_saved: Saved. The next collector run will use these.
assistant.waiting_collector_for: {{assistant}} is waiting for the {{collector}} collector — up to {{duration}} more.
assistant.waiting_unavailable: Collector waiting is unavailable while the System health feature is disabled.
assistant.waiting_arrived: New readings have landed. Anything you read before this is from before them — call the tools again rather than reasoning from the old answers.
assistant.waiting_timed_out: Nothing new arrived from the {{collector}} collector in that time. That is a finding: it is not running as often as it should, or at all. Say so rather than waiting again.
assistant.host_job_capabilities: Re-check what is installed on the host
assistant.host_job_capabilities_cost: Quick. Runs a handful of version checks.
assistant.host_job_disk_walk: Walk the whole filesystem as root
assistant.host_job_disk_walk_cost: Expensive — minutes on a large disk, and it reads the whole time.
assistant.host_request_why: {{cost}} It runs on the collector's next pass, not now.
assistant.host_request_why_reason: “{{reason}}” — {{cost}} It runs on the collector's next pass, not now.
assistant.host_request_explainer: This queues a job for the process running as root. Nothing runs in this window and nothing runs now.
assistant.host_request_unknown: There is no host job called “{{job}}”.
assistant.host_request_not_approved: Not approved — either declined or nobody answered. Treat it as a no, carry on with what you can see from this account, and say what you cannot answer because of it.
assistant.host_request_queued: Queued. It runs on the collector's next pass — use get_pending_host_requests to see whether it has landed, or wait_for_new_readings to wait for it. Do not assume the answer is available yet.
assistant.highlight_not_found: Nothing on the {{page}} page contains that text, so nothing was highlighted. The user may be on a different page — open_page first — or it may not be shown there at all. Do not describe a highlight that did not happen.
assistant.highlight_shown: It is outlined and pulsing for a few seconds. Say what you are pointing at in the same message; a highlight with no sentence is a poke.
ai.skip_question_help: Carry on without answering — the same as letting the clock run out
diagnosis.nothing_to_report: Nothing to report. Every check ran and none of them found anything — which is a different statement from nothing having been measured.
diagnosis.ignored_help: These are intentional exceptions. Restore one to include it in later checks.
